modules.name: Universal Audio Processor
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; LGE208 version by Low-Gain Electronics
modules.summary: Two VCAs with an equal-power control circuit, switchable between a dual VCA, a stereo panner and a voltage-controlled crossfader.
how_it_works: Inside are two voltage-controlled amplifiers and a small control circuit that drives them. The control circuit makes two complementary control signals: as one VCA opens, the other closes. Because the curve is equal-power rather than linear, the overall loudness stays the same as a sound moves between the two sides, with no dip in the middle.
The three-position switch changes how the audio is routed between the two VCAs, so one panel does three jobs without any patching:

PAN (up): one input signal feeds both VCAs. PAN / FADE and VC PAN move it between OUT 1 and OUT 2: a stereo panner. GAIN and VC 1+2 set the overall level. The arrows on the panel show which input is shared in each mode.
DUAL VCA (centre): the two VCAs work on their own. IN 1 goes to OUT 1 under VC 1, IN 2 to OUT 2 under VC 2: two separate amplifiers for envelopes, tremolo or gating.
XFADE (down): two different signals at IN 1 and IN 2 are blended under voltage control. PAN / FADE and VC PAN set the mix, and as one source rises the other falls.
AM 1 and AM 2 are AC-coupled inputs for amplitude modulation at audio rates, separate from the DC-coupled VC inputs. Each output appears on both a 1/4" jack and a banana.
controls: Each output on a 1/4" jack and a banana jack.

modules.name: Tri-Core VCO
modules.summary: A stable triangle-core VCO with sine, triangle and pulse outputs, exponential and linear FM, PWM, sync and a VCO / LFO range switch.
how_it_works: The heart of the oscillator is a triangle core: a capacitor is charged and discharged by a current that rises exponentially with the control voltage, so one volt more doubles the frequency. A comparator flips the direction each time the ramp hits its limits, giving a clean triangle wave and, from the comparator itself, a square wave.

The exponential converter uses a matched transistor pair kept stable by a 2k tempco resistor, which cancels the pair's drift with temperature; that is what makes the V/OCT tracking hold over five or six octaves. Trimmers set the V/OCT scale and the high-frequency tracking.

The sine is shaped from the triangle by a JFET waveshaper, with trimmers for its roundness and symmetry. The pulse output compares the triangle against a level set by PW and the PWM input, so the pulse width can be swept.

EXP FM (VC F on the panel) adds to the pitch exponentially, the musical way for vibrato and pitch modulation. LIN FM changes the frequency linearly, which keeps the pitch centred under audio-rate modulation for clean FM timbres. SYNC resets the core to lock it to another oscillator. The VCO / LFO switch drops the range for slow modulation, and the bi-colour LED shows the triangle swinging up and down.
controls: Summed pitch inputs, 1 volt per octave.

modules.name: VC Phaser
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS90 version by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A voltage-controlled phase shifter with three phase-shifted outputs and a built-in mix for the classic notched phasing sound.
how_it_works: The input runs through a chain of all-pass stages. An all-pass stage leaves the level of every frequency alone but delays its phase, and the amount of delay depends on frequency and on the control voltage. Taps along the chain give outputs shifted by 360°, 720° and 1080°.

On their own the shifted outputs sound almost the same as the input, because the ear hardly hears phase. The effect appears when a shifted signal is mixed back with the original: frequencies that come out of phase cancel, cutting a row of notches into the spectrum. The MIXED output does this inside the module with the 1080° tap, and the MIX knob sets the balance.
PHASE sets the shift by hand. The VC input, through its attenuator, sweeps it from an envelope, LFO or sequencer; the response follows a log curve so sweeps sound even across the range.

Ken Stone's CGS90 puts two small audio mixers on the same PCB. Each has three inputs with level knobs plus one unity-gain x1 input. They are inverting and AC coupled, which makes them good for blending the raw phase outputs with the dry signal (straight or inverted) and for feedback patches: mix the phaser's output with its input before it goes back in. Patch one mixer's output into the other's x1 input to get a single six-input mixer.
controls: Input mixed with the 1080° output: the phasing sound.

modules.name: Wave Multipliers
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS113 version by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Three separate voltage-controlled waveshapers that add harmonics to a signal instead of filtering them away.
how_it_works: A filter changes timbre by removing frequencies. The Wave Multipliers do the opposite: they bend the waveform so that new, harmonically related overtones appear. Each of the three sections works in a different way, and each has its own control voltage and knob. In a VCO-VCF-VCA patch the usual place for it is between the oscillator and the filter.

Top section: a switch picks the mode. In HI it squares up the signal with rounded, saturated peaks, like an overdriven tube amplifier but voltage controlled. In LO it is a plain linear VCA, handy for amplitude modulation or for gating a signal into the other sections.

Middle section: fed with a sine wave, turning it up sweeps through the odd harmonics, up to about the 13th. It sounds like overblowing a pipe closed at one end, so it suits reed and wind sounds. A second input lets two signals be mixed before processing, which gives sum-and-difference-like effects richer than a ring modulator.

Bottom section: chained full-wave rectifiers, each of which doubles the frequency of a sine or triangle. Sweeping the control moves smoothly through the even harmonics (2nd, 4th, 8th) without the drop in level a plain rectifier gives. It has two inputs and two outputs; the second output is a squared-up version of the first and behaves like a more complex pulse-width modulation.
controls: Control voltage and manual amount for that section.
Top section: linear VCA (LO) or soft squaring (HI).

modules.name: Dual Universal Slope Generator
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin; CGS114 version by Ken Stone
modules.summary: Two identical slope generators, each of which can be a slew limiter, envelope, LFO, audio oscillator or pulse divider.
how_it_works: Each half produces a voltage that rises and falls at rates set by the RISE and FALL knobs. What it does depends only on what is patched into it.

Slew: a voltage at IN is followed by the output, but no faster than the RISE and FALL times allow. With a stepped voltage at IN this gives portamento; with the knobs fully up the output simply copies the input.
Envelope: a pulse at TRIG IN starts a rise from 0 to about +5 V followed by the fall. A new trigger during the envelope is ignored, and an END pulse comes out when the cycle finishes.

Oscillator: patch END back to TRIG IN (or set the cycle switch where fitted) and the slope runs continuously, from slow LFO up to audio. With RISE and FALL equal it makes a triangle; making one much shorter turns it into a sawtooth.

Pitch and control: 1V/OCT halves the rise and fall times for each added volt, so the slope tracks a keyboard. VC IN, through its attenuator, varies the times too, and the switch chooses whether VC acts on RISE, FALL or BOTH.
Divider: feed a pulse train into TRIG IN with a cycle a little longer than the pulse spacing, and the generator skips pulses, producing sub-harmonics.
controls: Pulse at the end of each cycle (LED shows activity).
Control of the times, with attenuator.

modules.name: VC Filter (1973)
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin, 1973; CGS77 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A two-pole state-variable resonant filter with simultaneous low-pass, band-pass and high-pass outputs.
how_it_works: A state-variable filter: one circuit produces low-pass, band-pass and high-pass versions of the input at the same time, each on its own output. All three share one cutoff frequency and one resonance (Q).
The cutoff is set by a knob and by voltage control; Q sets how strongly the filter rings at the cutoff. The original uses CA3080 transconductance amplifiers for the voltage-controlled stages.
Prism's calibration starts with a sawtooth into the audio input and the cutoff fully down, listening at the low-pass output.

modules.name: Resonant Equalizer
modules.designer: Serge Tcherepnin, 1982; CGS202 by Ken Stone
modules.summary: A ten-band fixed filter bank whose bands can boost, cut or ring, with two comb outputs carrying alternate bands.

modules.name: Wave Multiplier (CGS29)
modules.designer: Ken Stone, after the middle section of the Serge Wave Multipliers
modules.summary: A wave folder modelled on the middle section of the Serge Wave Multipliers: folds a signal into harmonically rich shapes.
how_it_works: As the input level rises, the circuit folds the waveform back on itself again and again, adding harmonics; sweeping the level or a control voltage moves the sound like a filter, but brighter.

Ken Stone designed it from descriptions and scope traces of the Serge module; the result is close, except the last fold keeps more of the original shape. The two-input panel mixes A and B before the folder.

modules.name: Band Pass Filters
modules.summary: Manually tuned band-pass filters with frequency and Q knobs, for fixed resonances and formants.
how_it_works: Each filter passes a band around its centre frequency; the Q knob makes the band narrower and more resonant. Several in parallel set up the fixed resonances of a virtual instrument body or vocal formants.
The outputs are summed to a shared output with a gain control, and an aux input joins the sum.

modules.name: Sub Oscillator
modules.summary: A two-channel sub-oscillator: divides a VCO by 2, 4 and 8 (and 3, 5 or 7) for fat bass, harmonies or pattern sequences.
how_it_works: Each channel divides an incoming oscillator into lower octaves and odd sub-harmonics with prescale switches, and mixes them by knob into its output.
Driven by two VCOs it fattens or harmonises a line; driven by a VCO and an LFO it steps through harmonic sequences.

modules.name: Utility LFO
modules.summary: Two LFOs with variable shape (falling ramp through triangle to rising ramp), variable pulse width and a mixed output.
how_it_works: Each LFO is an integrator and Schmitt trigger; the shape knob moves the ramp from falling saw through triangle to rising saw and the pulse width with it, and a fixed square is also available.
The VARIABLE output mixes between the saw/triangle and the square. JOIN and SWAP switches cross-connect the two LFOs' variable outputs.

modules.name: Dual CMOS Filter
modules.designer: Ken Stone, after the EDP Wasp filter
modules.summary: Two filters built on CMOS inverters, after the EDP Wasp, with adjustable post-filter distortion.
how_it_works: Each filter core is made of CMOS logic inverters running between 0 and -5 V, which gives the gritty, unstable character of the Wasp; a simple exponential converter sets the frequency from the control voltage.
After the filter a distortion stage is blended with the clean signal, so each channel can go from smooth to fuzzy.
controls: Cross-connect the two filters' input and CV (+ / -).
